common_name: Grace Stewart Winter Daphne (New Zealand Breeding-Line Fragrant Daphne)

planting.note: Plant in early fall or spring in sharply drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; choose the permanent site carefully, since this winter daphne selection resents being moved once established.

directions: Grace Stewart is a New Zealand-raised selection of winter daphne best known today as a breeding parent behind larger-flowered hybrid daphnes rather than as a widely sold garden plant in its own right. Like other forms of D. odora, it carries glossy, dark evergreen leaves and dense clusters of intensely sweet-scented, rosy-pink-and-cream flowers that open from midwinter into early spring, well before most other shrubs bloom. Site it in humus-rich, sharply drained, slightly acidic soil in part shade and leave it undisturbed once planted, since daphnes resent root disturbance. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so keep it away from areas where children or pets forage.

common_name: Pale Moon Azalea (Pale Cream Native Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this Aromi sibling of 'Moon Dreams' and 'High Tide' carries the palest flower color of the group.

directions: Pale Moon is one of several pale, moon-themed Aromi azaleas raised from the same OF-1 x 'Centerpiece' cross that produced Moon Dreams, High Tide, and Peach Glow, each selected for subtle differences in blotch strength and petal flush. Its flowers open in the faintest cream to near-white tone with only a whisper of yellow at the throat, giving a softer, more luminous look than its more strongly blotched siblings. Like the rest of this breeding line, it carries the heat and humidity tolerance inherited from native Rhododendron austrinum parentage on a rounded, well-branched deciduous shrub. Plant in humus-rich, acidic, evenly moist soil in partial shade, and mulch to protect the shallow roots through Gulf Coast summers.
sources: Azalea Society of America — Aromi Deciduous Azaleas
Journal American Rhododendron Society, v56n1 — The Aromi Azaleas

common_name: Elmer's Yellow Azalea (Golden Fragrant Native Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this Aromi hybrid was later used alongside 'Fool's Folly' as a parent of 'Centerpiece'.

directions: Elmer's Yellow is remembered today chiefly as one of the two parents, alongside 'Fool's Folly', behind the widely grown Aromi hybrid Centerpiece. Its name points to clear golden-yellow flowers in the fragrant, open-faced style typical of Rhododendron austrinum-derived Aromi breeding stock, carried in rounded trusses during the heavy spring flush characteristic of this line. As with its relatives, it forms a medium, well-branched deciduous shrub that tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity far better than Exbury or Knap Hill azaleas grown on their own roots. Site it in humus-rich, acidic, consistently moist soil in partial shade, and avoid heavy pruning since next year's flower buds set on the current season's growth.
sources: Azalea Society of America — Aromi Deciduous Azaleas
The Azalean (2003) — Named Aromi Deciduous Hybrids chart
Journal American Rhododendron Society, v56n1 — The Aromi Azaleas

common_name: Pirate's Pink Azalea (Unscented Deep Pink-Red Native Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in morning sun with afternoon shade; this sibling of 'Pirate's Booty' shares its unscented flowers.

directions: Pirate's Pink is a sibling selection to Pirate's Booty, both raised from Frontier Red in Dr. Eugene Aromi's breeding program and both notable for lacking the fragrance typical of most native-derived azalea hybrids. Its flowers open in rich pink-red tones carried over from the bold two-tone coloring established earlier in the Frontier Red line, blooming in the same heavy spring flush as its Aromi relatives. The deciduous shrub forms a medium, well-branched habit suited to a sunny woodland edge in Gulf Coast gardens. Plant in humus-rich, acidic soil with morning sun and afternoon shade, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds set on the previous year's growth.
sources: Azalea Society of America — Aromi Deciduous Azaleas
Journal American Rhododendron Society, v56n1 — The Aromi Azaleas

common_name: Indian Spring Azalea (Yellow and Red Native Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this descendant of 'Frontier Red' carries a yellow-and-red bicolor bloom.

directions: Indian Spring descends from Frontier Red in Dr. Eugene Aromi's native azalea breeding program and carries a bold yellow-and-red bicolor pattern inherited from that parentage, distinct from the plain red-orange of Frontier Red itself. It blooms in the same heavy spring flush typical of the Aromi line, on a deciduous shrub with the vigor and open, upright habit common to Rhododendron austrinum-derived hybrids. Grow in humus-rich, acidic, evenly moist soil in partial shade, mulching well to protect the shallow root system through Gulf Coast summer heat. Prune only right after flowering, since next year's buds set on the current season's growth.
sources: Azalea Society of America — Aromi Deciduous Azaleas
Journal American Rhododendron Society, v56n1 — The Aromi Azaleas

common_name: Pendent Silver Linden (Weeping Fragrant Shade Tree)

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown nursery stock in spring in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; this old weeping form of silver linden was a parent of the Morton Arboretum's 'Centennial' street-tree selection.

directions: Pendent silver linden is an old European selection of silver linden grown for its gracefully drooping outer branches, which cascade from a broad, rounded crown in a way the upright straight species never does. Its dark green leaves share the species' silvery, felted undersides, flashing bright white whenever wind moves the canopy, and its fragrant creamy flowers draw heavy bee traffic in early summer. It needs generous room to mature into a large specimen tree and is best used on parks, campuses, or large residential lots rather than tight urban strips. Plant in well-drained, fertile loam in full sun, and expect the same strong drought tolerance and aphid resistance that makes silver linden a durable shade tree once established.

common_name: Lady Foster Bearded Iris (Historic 1900s Foster Blue Bitone Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil; Lady Foster is the sibling seedling for which Sir Michael Foster's better-documented 'Shelford Chieftain' was named a companion.

directions: Lady Foster was raised by British physiologist and amateur iris breeder Sir Michael Foster in the early 1900s, a sibling seedling to his better-known Shelford Chieftain and sharing the same medium-blue, bitone coloring that came from his pioneering crosses of Iris cypriana and Iris trojana into early Iris pallida breeding lines. Though it never achieved the historical fame of its sibling, it represents the same foundational blue bearded iris stock that underpins much of the modern tall bearded iris class. Set rhizomes shallowly with the top exposed to full sun in well-drained soil, and divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigorous flowering.
